extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, judges, practitioners, and advanced law students interested in administrative law, separation of powers, and judicial review of executive action
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and doctrinal framing of a category of executive action—'enforcement lawmaking'—and how federal courts have responded; identifies attributes, examples, and the judicial practices that shape review. Useful for evaluating when executive acts amount to lawmaking via enforcement and how courts treat such actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement lawmaking (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President — or a high-level executive official motivated by the President — directs action in a top-down fashion intended to use enforcement discretion to enact broad policy goals, often incorporating presidential administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement lawmaking 'uses enforcement discretion built into legislative enactments in a way that meaningfully transforms enforcement into something more than enforcement policy.' It is executed through executive orders, declarations, enforcement memoranda, letters to high-level officials, and administrative actions; it can countermand or substitute for stalled legislation. Line-drawing is fuzzy; some actions may be mere attempts at enforcement lawmaking if courts resist them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments and modalities of enforcement lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms through which enforcement lawmaking is carried out: executive orders, presidential declarations, memoranda, enforcement memoranda, 'Dear Colleague' letters, conditions on grants, certifications under federal statutes, and administrative rulemaking or policy instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article lists these instruments explicitly as the mechanisms by which the Executive "has enacted broad policy changes in a manner that shares attributes of policy, law, and enforcement." Examples: DACA (memorandum), transgender bathroom policy (Dear Colleague letter), sanctuary-cities conditions (EO + AG conditions + §1373 certification), census citizenship question (administrative action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria distinguishing enforcement lawmaking from ordinary administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement lawmaking goes beyond individual enforcement decisions and shares attributes with legislation; it attempts to effectuate broad policy choices rather than case-by-case enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the action: (1) uses enforcement discretion to enact broad policy goals; (2) operates top-down under presidential direction; (3) uses the administrative state to shape policy; (4) seeks to fill or countermand legislative gaps; and (5) produces effects akin to law rather than routine administrative action. The Article excludes certain domains (criminal law, foreign affairs, routine admin action) from its focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fragility and reversibility of enforcement lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement lawmaking is 'fragile and subject to reversal with a change in administration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it often relies on executive discretion and administrative instruments rather than durable statutory enactments, such measures can be undone or reversed by successor administrations, a factual characteristic that affects how courts and scholars should view their legal status and permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial borrowing of statutory-canons and statutory tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts assessing enforcement lawmaking sometimes 'borrow judicially crafted canons and tools of statutory interpretation' to evaluate executive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial reliance on legislative canons reveals how enforcement lawmaking shares attributes with legislation; courts sometimes treat executive-originated measures as if they were statutes (and at times even refer to them as 'statutes' or 'legislation'). This practice shapes the review framework and outcomes in cases challenging enforcement lawmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' formalist vs. functionalist approach to separation-of-powers questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts often rely on formalist, rather than functionalist, conceptions of the separation of powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formalist approach may make courts less likely to check executive power in systemic ways, while a functionalist approach might produce different scrutiny. The Article notes that reliance on formalism contributes to judicial reluctance to curb executive expansion in many contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial deference and reliance on agency expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts frequently defer to administrative agencies and rely on agencies' expertise in adjudicating disputes involving executive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference doctrines and faith in agency expertise are identified as practices that generally facilitate executive power and influence courts' willingness to invalidate enforcement-lawmaking actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of regularity as a judicial practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'presumption of regularity' gives federal actors the benefit of the doubt by presuming that their actions are taken in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article identifies this lesser-studied judicial practice as one that dignifies and protects executive-branch litigants, making it more difficult for challengers to prove improper motive or irregularity in enforcement-lawmaking contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial avoidance of politically charged disputes (political-question avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts avoid adjudicating matters they deem 'clearly political', invoking doctrines that eschew judicial review in such contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoidance reduces courts' role as a check on certain forms of executive action, particularly where issues implicate core political functions or national-security/war powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors and institutional sources of countervailing checks
rubrics_metrics.description: States, intra-executive actors (e.g., career civil servants, agency litigators), political parties, and even Congress can act as counters to executive enforcement lawmaking by using litigation and other mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of checks: states seeking injunctions (e.g., Hawai’i v. Trump), intra-executive refusals to defend or 'bare-bones' justifications (DACA), party control leading to suits (House suing over ACA implementation). The Article emphasizes that these actors often act 'with and through the federal courts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of presidential-administration mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms of presidential control — centralization in the Executive Office, 'pooling' agency resources, appointing politically aligned agency personnel, using 'acting officials', and informal legal advisors — increase presidential influence over the administrative state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices (collectively discussed under 'presidential administration' and related concepts like 'porous legalism' and 'pooling powers') are identified as signals that the Executive is reconfiguring agencies to achieve enforcement-lawmaking objectives; they complicate Congress's oversight role and affect judicial assessment of executive action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-drawing challenges in identifying enforcement lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The boundaries of the category 'enforcement lawmaking' are 'concededly fuzzy' and hard to draw in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article cautions that determining whether a given executive action constitutes enforcement lawmaking versus ordinary administrative governance may be debatable, and that the goal is to delineate a general category rather than produce a perfect taxonomy. This fuzziness affects doctrinal analysis and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of enforcement threats or non-self-enforcing guidance to induce compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that are not self-enforcing (e.g., 'Dear Colleague' letters) can use the specter of enforcement (loss of funding, conditions) to nudge compliance by regulated entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transgender bathroom 'Dear Colleague' letter is an example: the policy informed school districts they risked losing Title IX-linked funding unless they complied. Such 'nudges' are a tactic of enforcement lawmaking distinct from formal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial treatment of source-of-law ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts sometimes are not conscious about the source of law they analyze and may conflate executive action with statutes when applying interpretive tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conflation (explicit in cases like County of Santa Clara v. Trump) affects the doctrinal apparatus applied and may either magnify or limit judicial scrutiny depending on which statutory canons or constitutional tests are borrowed.
